title: Will Marion Cook's unpaid band in Philadelphia
summary: On the way home Howard worked for Will Marion Cook, who did not pay the band until comedian Speedy Smith threatened him.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: I mean, the only thing that worried me, I got homesick. And, and, and on the way home, I went to, I went to work with Will May and Cook.
On the way home, what do you mean?
I went to work with Will May and Cook. And he didn't pay off the band. Now, that was the experience.
Go ahead. Come in. She's on me.
Oh. In fact, you just leave it there.

So, so, Speedy Smith, a comedian, he said, by God, he says, how much do you owe you? I said, you know, me, I'm all in my money. He said, I'm going to get some of them. I said, don't worry about it. I think you'll get some money. He went in there. And I remember hearing him say, man, Cook, if you don't give me my money, I'm going to blow your damn brains out. Yeah. I get him. And I heard something like him putting a gun on. And I heard something like him putting a gun on. You know, he came out and gave me $16. I don't know how much he got, but I got $16. So, I went and stayed at a place called Mama Charleston where my mother and aunt used to stay in Philadelphia. She fed us, boarded, you know, slept. Mama Charleston says, well, says, I know your mama so well, says, I'm going to speak to a fellow. Says, I know you don't want to stay around Philadelphia. I'm going to speak to a fellow that works on, you know, one of his gangs on the road and see if I can get you a pass. Five dollars, she got me a pass for. I gave the man five dollars. And the pass didn't have a destination on it. He says, when you get on this train, says, you don't ask any questions. You know where you're going. Yeah. That's okay. Because if you have to ask questions, you have no business with the pass. I won't forget that. So, I get on this train. Get there to Pittsburgh. Track 10 is Chicago and track 12 is Wheeling, West Virginia. I guess on track 12. I know, ooh, that was awful. Ride all night. About 8 o'clock in the morning, the man says, Wheeling, West Virginia, far as we go. And that's the first time I knew I was going the wrong direction. Really? Oh, man, it was awful. And my trunk is in Chicago and I'm in Wheeling, West Virginia. All I got is my fiddle up in the, you know, bloody scare. Didn't have no birth. I don't know. Well, all I did was went to the telephone. I had about time I got through eating and carrying on, you know, odds and ends. I had a dollar, eating some hundred cents in my pocket to my name. Sent my mother telegram. Well, sure, I don't know no difference. I told her to send me a ticket. Quite nicely, she sent me just what I asked for. Sent me money for the ticket. Nothing extra. Nothing less. I'm down about 35 cents. I'm having a heck of a time. The train pulls out at 710 and the bag on telegram comes to 725. I got 35 cents to my name. So the baggage man that had been there that morning, he knew the predicament I was in. He comes to work that night and says, you still here? I says, I am. He says, well, I imagine you spend some money. I said, oh yeah, I got about 35 cents to my name. He said, are you sleepy? I said, no, not now. He said, when you do, he says, you get up on those trunks. He says, I got a sandwich. When I eat, I'll call you down. And sure enough, he did. Now, when I was with Earl Hines, I was 30. No, it wasn't with Earl Hines. It was Plantation Days, a show. We went to Pittsburgh. I tried to find that man. I wanted to reimburse him. Yes. That was pretty nice, you know. Sure. But he had retired. He didn't know where it was. That was 1923. Well, that was the hardest experience.
